description: Somos Lagrange Riff, un equipo de Piura de estudiantes de Física, Ingeniería Aeroespacial e Ingeniería Ambiental. Abordamos el reto Lunar Landing Site Navigator: con modelos matemáticos y geometría calculamos la posición del Sol y la Tierra sobre el horizonte del polo sur lunar, para comparar sitios y fechas según energía solar y comunicación directa. Nos mueve la pasión por las matemáticas y la física. Usamos IA como herramienta y la declararemos en la entrega.
summary: At the lunar south pole, where the next missions want to land, the Sun never climbs more than about 2° above the horizon. A single ridge or a one-week delay decides whether a lander has power and a line of sight to Earth. Lunar Landing Site Navigator is a free web app that answers the planner's question for any site and any date: when will we have sunlight, and when can we talk to Earth? It computes the elevation and azimuth of the Sun and Earth hour by hour from any point on the Moon and compares up to three sites side by side: time with Sun, time with Earth in view, longest night, longest communication blackout, solar panel energy and a viability index. It animates the view from the surface, maps illumination around the pole, scores every start date and ranks more than 16,000 locations for solar power in under a second. The geometry matches NASA JPL Horizons to 0.001°, and the terrain at Peak near Shackleton is calibrated against NASA's LOLA illumination maps. It runs in any browser, in English, Spanish and Chinese, for mission planners, students and the public.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Lunar Landing Site Navigator answers the mission planner's question: "If we land here on this date, when do we have power and when can we talk to Earth?" The user picks up to three sites (Apollo sites, CLPS landings such as IM-1, IM-2 and Blue Ghost M1, the upcoming IM-3 target, Chandrayaan-3, Chang'e 4 and 6, south pole craters, 11 points our team measured in LROC QuickMap, or any custom coordinates), a start date and an analysis window from 7 days to 1 year. The app then shows:

- A realistic view from the surface with the Sun, Earth (with its true phase) and the local horizon, plus countdowns to the next sunset, sunrise, Earthset and Earthrise.

- Site cards with % time with Sun, % time with Earth in view, % time with both, longest night, longest communication blackout, solar panel energy (kWh), peak power (W) and a viability index with adjustable weights.

- An animated timeline (6 hours/s to 3 days/s) shared by every view.

- A south pole illumination map with the terminator sweeping around the pole.

- A calendar that scores every start day of the next 30 days, so a slipped launch can be re-planned in seconds.

- An optimizer that ranks more than 16,000 lunar locations for solar power in under a second.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Ephemerides: Sun and Moon positions from the open-source Astronomy Engine library, computed in the browser.

2. Lunar orientation: vectors are rotated into the Moon-fixed frame with the IAU (WGCCRE 2009) rotation model, which includes physical libration.

3. Local sky: elevation from sin h = û · ŝ, measured from the site itself (topocentric); azimuth from north through east; no atmosphere, so no refraction.

4. Visibility: the Sun counts when its upper limb clears the local horizon; Earth counts when its center clears the horizon plus an optional minimum antenna elevation.

5. Terrain: each site has a constant horizon or a direction-dependent mask. At Peak near Shackleton the mask shape comes from 8 LOLA elevation points measured around the peak (H = arctan(Δz/d) − d/2R), and its level is shifted until the model reproduces the yearly illumination measured by NASA's LOLA polar map (28%).

6. Power: P = A · η · S · cos θ · v · (1 − f_eclipse), with S = 1361 W/m² scaled by the Sun distance, for horizontal, vertical (best azimuth) or Sun-tracking panels; lunar eclipses are modeled as Earth covering the solar disc.

7. Optimizer: a Web Worker evaluates a 2° global grid plus the catalog sites at 1-hour steps and ranks them by energy and longest night.

VALIDATION AGAINST NASA DATA

- Sun and Earth from Shackleton crater vs. JPL Horizons (DE441), 73 hourly points: max difference 0.001° in elevation, 0.004° in azimuth.

- Sun from the Apollo 11 site vs. JPL Horizons, 25 hourly points: max difference 0.004° in elevation, 0.001° in azimuth.

- Yearly illumination at Peak near Shackleton: model 28.0%, NASA LOLA map 28.0%.

- Lunar eclipses of 3 Mar 2026, 28 Aug 2026 and 20 Feb 2027 detected at the correct times.

WHAT WE FOUND

The date matters as much as the site. At the summit of Peak near Shackleton, a 7-day mission starting 15 November 2026 has sunlight 40% of the time; the same mission starting 2 December 2026 has 100%. Seventeen days change everything, and the app shows it in one click.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

When a launch slips or hardware changes, engineers can test alternative dates or nearby sites in seconds instead of navigating several expert tools. The same views explain to students and the public why the lunar poles are so hard: a Sun that skims the horizon, an Earth that barely moves, and nights that last for weeks. The app is free, needs no installation and works in English, Spanish and Chinese.

LIMITATIONS (also stated in the app)

- The global grid in the optimizer uses a smooth horizon and ignores terrain shadows.

- At Peak near Shackleton the horizon shape comes from LOLA points 40 km away; nearby terrain enters only through the calibration. Other measured points use a constant equivalent horizon, which overstates the longest night near the pole.

- Catalog coordinates are approximate.

- Rocks, craters and the lander in the surface view are illustrative; the horizon line and the Sun and Earth positions are computed.

Next steps: compute horizon masks directly from LOLA elevation models and check Earth visibility against terrain for direct-to-Earth antennas.

TOOLS

HTML, CSS and JavaScript (Canvas 2D, Web Workers), Astronomy Engine, Node.js and Playwright for testing, FFmpeg for the demo video, Netlify for hosting. No server: the whole app is a single HTML file.

USE OF AI

We used Claude (Anthropic), DeepSeek and ChatGPT (OpenAI) as assistants to write the application code, draft the mathematical write-up, the video script and these texts, review ideas and design the team logo. The demo video narration is an AI-generated voice (Kokoro text-to-speech) reading our script; this is stated on screen and in the video file's metadata, and the video was assembled with AI assistance from a real screen recording of the app. The team chose the challenge and the approach, gathered the NASA data (LROC QuickMap illumination and elevation readings, JPL Horizons tables), validated the results and reviewed all content. No NASA logos or branding are used; the background and surface view are code-drawn illustrations.

TEAM

Lagrange Riff, Piura, Peru: Sebastián Silva (physics), Tomás Atarama (aerospace engineering), Lucio Pozo (environmental engineering).
